summary: A constitutional monarchy in Western Europe where the Dutch-speaking north and the French-speaking south coexist; its capital, Brussels, is home to the headquarters of the European Union and NATO.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Belgian region was Christianized around the 7th century by missionaries such as Saint Amand; during the Reformation in the 16th century the Spanish Habsburgs suppressed Protestantism in the Southern Netherlands and many Protestants fled north to the Netherlands, making the south (today's Belgium) a Catholic region. Belgium became independent in 1830, partly because the Catholic south opposed the rule of the Protestant Dutch king. In the late 20th century secularization accelerated, and together with church sexual abuse scandals the Catholic share has fallen to about half, with few regular churchgoers.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown rapidly since the war; Belgium has a deep tradition of free thought, and the Free University of Brussels, founded in 1834, was established with the purpose of independence from the church. The 1993 constitutional revision formally recognized that organizations of 'non-confessional philosophical life stances' can receive the same state funding as religions, and secularization is especially noticeable in Brussels and Wallonia.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived in large numbers in the 1960s when Belgium signed labor recruitment agreements with Morocco (1964) and Turkey (1964); the migrant workers mostly worked in mines and factories, and their families later also moved to Belgium. Belgium formally recognized Islam in 1974, and today Muslims are concentrated in cities such as Brussels, Antwerp and Ghent.

ranking.name: Protestantism and other Christians
ranking.description: Protestantism was once prevalent in cities such as Antwerp in the 16th century, but the suppression by the Spanish rulers made believers flee in large numbers, and it has been a minority ever since. Today's Protestants include the long-established United Protestant Church in Belgium and the evangelical churches that have grown in recent years with African and Latin American immigrants.

religion.background: Christianity reached the Belgian region at the end of the Roman period, and in the Middle Ages this was a prosperous belt of Catholic commercial cities. The Reformation of the 16th century caused conflict with the Spanish rulers, and in the end the northern Netherlands became independent as a Protestant country, while the south remained in Spanish hands and stayed Catholic. When Belgium became independent from the Netherlands in 1830, Catholics and liberals founded the state together, but the 'school war' between the two camps over education continued until it ended with an agreement in 1958. Today Belgium officially recognizes Catholicism, Protestantism, Judaism, Anglicanism, Islam, Orthodoxy and organizations of non-confessional philosophical life stances, and the state pays the salaries of the clergy.

language.official: The official languages are Dutch, French and German.

ranking.name: Dutch (Flemish)
ranking.description: Dutch (called Flemish in Belgium) is the mother tongue of the inhabitants of the northern region of Flanders; when cities such as Ghent and Bruges flourished in the Middle Ages, they were mainly Dutch-dialect speaking. After independence in 1830 French was the only language of the upper class, and the Flemish fought for their rights through the 'Flemish Movement'; in 1898 Dutch gained equal legal status with French, and in 1930 Ghent University switched to teaching in Dutch. Because the Flemish population is larger, about 60 percent of the population speak it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French is spoken in the southern region of Wallonia and in the capital, Brussels. In the 19th century the Belgian aristocracy, bourgeoisie and government all used French, and the coal and iron industry of Wallonia also made it the economic center; Brussels was gradually 'Frenchified' from a Dutch-speaking city in the 19th and 20th centuries. The language border laws of 1962-1963 divided the country into different language areas, and French speakers make up about four tenths of the population.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: German is spoken in the German-speaking Community in the east (around Eupen and Sankt Vith), an area that originally belonged to Prussia and was assigned to Belgium by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 after World War I, and was annexed by Nazi Germany during World War II. Because it has only a little over seventy thousand inhabitants, German speakers make up about 1 percent, but it has its own parliament and government.

language.history: Belgium lies on the dividing line between the Germanic and Romance languages, a linguistic boundary that had roughly formed by the time the Franks settled in the 5th century: the north speaks Dutch dialects and the south speaks French dialects (Walloon, Picard). After independence in 1830, French became the language of the government, the army and the upper class, which prompted the Flemish Movement, in which Dutch speakers long fought for equality. The legal language border was drawn in 1962-1963, and from 1970 a series of constitutional revisions gradually turned Belgium into a federal state based on language communities, formally becoming a federation in 1993. Today Brussels is a bilingual French-Dutch region, and language issues still deeply affect Belgian politics.

ranking.name: Moules-Frites
ranking.description: A large pot of mussels steamed with white wine, onion, celery and butter, served with twice-fried golden fries and often a glass of Belgian beer.
ranking.history: The Belgian North Sea coast has long been rich in mussels, which from the 19th century became a cheap source of protein for the poor, while fries were already sold on Belgian streets in the late 19th century. The combination 'moules-frites' became popular in small restaurants in Brussels in the early 20th century and later became a national dish. Belgians consider that they invented fries, and the term 'French fries' is said to come from American soldiers stationed in Belgium during World War I, because the people of the local French-speaking region spoke French.

ranking.name: Belgian Waffles
ranking.description: Waffles baked in a grid mold from a yeasted batter or a dough with sugar pearls, divided into the light rectangular Brussels waffle and the round, sweet Liège waffle.
ranking.history: Grid waffles already existed in medieval Europe, originally cakes baked in iron molds for church festivals. The Liège waffle is said to originate with the cook of the Prince-Bishop of Liège in the 18th century, with pearl sugar added to the dough so that the outside caramelizes when baked. The Brussels waffle attracted international attention at the Brussels World's Fair of 1958, and at the New York World's Fair of 1964 it became popular in the United States under the name 'Belgian waffle'.

ranking.name: Carbonnade Flamande
ranking.description: Pieces of beef are slowly stewed with dark Belgian beer, onion, mustard and spice bread; the sauce is rich with a sweet-and-sour taste, and it is often eaten with fries.
ranking.history: Carbonnade is a traditional dish of Flanders and reflects Belgium's long brewing culture: since the Middle Ages monastery and town breweries have been found throughout the country, and Trappist abbey beers still exist today. Using beer instead of wine to stew the meat is because the Flemish climate is not suited to growing grapes. Adding spice bread (peperkoek) spread with mustard to thicken the sauce is a local specialty.

ranking.name: Waterzooi
ranking.description: Chicken or fish is stewed with leeks, carrots and potatoes, and the broth is thickened with egg yolk and cream into a rich, smooth creamy soup, somewhere between a soup and a stew.
ranking.history: Waterzooi originated in the Flemish city of Ghent, and its name comes from the Dutch 'water' and 'zooien' (to boil). The earliest version used freshwater fish caught in the rivers and canals flowing through Ghent, and only later, when river pollution reduced the fish, was chicken used instead. Ghent in the Middle Ages was one of the largest cities in Western Europe, and this dish is also seen as a source of pride for the people of Ghent. It is said that Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor born in Ghent in the 16th century, was also fond of it.

ranking.name: Stoemp
ranking.description: Potatoes are boiled together with vegetables such as carrots, leeks, spinach or cabbage and then mashed, often served with sausage, bacon or a cutlet.
ranking.history: Stoemp is a humble home dish of Brussels, and its name comes from the Brussels dialect and is related to the Dutch 'stomen' (to stew). Potatoes only became common in Belgium in the 18th century, and because of their high yield and cold tolerance they quickly became a staple of the working class. In the industrialization of the 19th century it was a cheap and filling dinner for workers' families, and today it is regarded as a nostalgic traditional dish of Brussels.
